text: An aircraft built to outrun its own sound has one flaw that only appears in an emergency: it cannot pull over. Made for American television, this is a disaster picture staged on the maiden flight of the country's first supersonic transport, and it doubles the trouble deliberately — sabotage has put the landing in question, and a flu loose in the cabin turns the passengers into a second crisis that no engineer can bolt shut. Eighty-nine minutes buys a cockpit, a cabin, and a room of men on the ground with a radio and a diagram, cut against each other as the fuel goes down. The pleasure is procedural. Nobody solves anything alone here, and most of the drama is people arguing a decision out loud before someone has to sign for it.

Two cars meet nose to nose in an alley too narrow for either to pass, and neither woman puts hers in reverse. That is the engine of the entire film. Rosa and Clara have lost their way in Palermo on a Sunday afternoon; Samira arrives from the far end with the Calafiore family packed into her seats; the sirocco goes on blowing. What starts as an obstruction hardens into a siege conducted through a windscreen — no eating, no drinking, no sleeping, no explanation offered to anybody — while the men of the street gather round and treat the whole thing as sport. Emma Dante keeps the comedy and the menace inside one frame, because the two drivers are the only people present who grasp that this can finish badly. Ninety minutes, one street, and rules nobody ever agreed to.

Johnnie Byrne holds a seat in the House of Commons and has reached his forties with almost nothing else in working order. The trouble is ordinary, which is exactly why he cannot get out from under it: a career stalled at a point where he can still see where it was going, a private life that keeps coming apart in his hands, and an election arriving on its own schedule whether or not he is ready. Then a woman he wants more than he wants the seat. The film sets the two appetites against each other and declines to make either one noble — the affair does not redeem him, the ambition does not damn him, and both take their time out of the same day. A hundred and ten minutes is long enough to watch a man run the same calculation twice and reach a different answer.

She married him for the pine trees, and the man came with them. Bernard owns the forest — along with the estate, the servants and a family name he intends to keep unblemished — and his conversation is property. The house stands well outside the town. What she wanted out of the match she received, which is the part the film will not let her off. Georges Franju tells the story backward, from a charge already laid, so the interest never rests on what Thérèse is accused of but on how an ordinary provincial marriage delivers a woman to that point. Her one warmth goes to Anne, her husband's half-sister, and there is little else in the house to spend it on. A hundred and nine minutes, cool the whole way through, with daily routine doing work another film would have handed to a villain.

A man crossing a street recognizes a woman selling goods from a stall, and it costs him the rest of the day. He is an officer, out of the war and into a marriage that suits him. She was at the front as well; the father of her small daughter was killed there, and she is bringing the girl up alone. What comes back to him is not desire but gratitude and tenderness, feelings harder to act on than desire and far harder to explain at home. Pyotr Todorovskiy moves between the front and the present without making either of them romantic, and the scale stays domestic throughout: a stall, a doorway, a conversation that has to end. Ninety-two minutes in which nobody behaves contemptibly and every decent impulse takes something from a third person.

A pastor shelters a blind young woman under his own roof, and for a long while that is simply charity. Then it is not, and the man least able to say so is the one who took her in. His son wants her too. From that point every kindness in the house can be read twice — the ones performed before anything was admitted, and the ones performed after — and Jean Delannoy lets the second reading arrive slowly, at table, in a corridor, in the pause before an answer. The crisis, when it comes, is entirely verbal. Nothing here is destroyed except a man's account of himself, and the film holds to that scale for a hundred and ten minutes. In his mouth, charity is not quite a lie; it is the last word left that his son cannot argue with.

Archimède wants to be arrested before the cold comes, and cannot manage it. Prison is warm and free, so the plan requires an offence large enough to earn a cell and modest enough to leave a man his dignity — a bureaucratic problem, essentially, and the film treats it as one. Seventy-nine minutes is a comic runtime, and this comedy runs on the discovery that a society is not eager to punish someone who is asking for it. The joke is never that the tramp is pitiful. It is that every institution he approaches would rather move him along than take responsibility for him, so each attempt has to be louder than the last. Underneath the routine, an account accumulates of who is permitted to be a nuisance and for how long. The cold is not a metaphor. It is the deadline.

A man starts doing favours for his new employer and finishes by handing over his house. The favours are small at first and nothing is ever demanded outright; that is the mechanism. He works in Parisian advertising, a trade where being available is already a virtue, and he mistakes being needed for being chosen — friends fall away, the family evenings empty out, and he describes each surrender as a privilege granted to him. His wife is the only one who keeps her distance and keeps watching. What she sees is pitiable and predatory at once, and she has no single word that covers both, which is the film's actual subject. The Louis Delluc Prize went to it. A hundred and five minutes, almost all of them in offices and living rooms, where the takeover is conducted entirely through kindness.

The school does not exist yet, which is the whole of the assignment: one demobilized Red Army soldier, one village in the Kyrgyz mountains, 1923. The children are forbidden to attend. The state that sent him is a very long way off, and the doctrine he carries is one he has never had reason to doubt, so what the setup produces is not enlightenment on schedule but a collision of two certainties — one backed by a new government, the other by everything the village has always done. Then he falls in love with a pupil, and her father sells her to a chieftain who can pay. Andrei Konchalovsky was making a Soviet film about Soviet arrival, and he is unsentimental about the price of it, particularly the price paid by the people being improved.

Trieste, the early 1900s: a factory belonging to an uncle, and a nephew on the payroll who is expected to be grateful. Ernesto is young, Italian, Jewish, and not settled about what he wants. The affair he begins is with one of his uncle's workers, which makes it a question of wages and standing before it is a question of scandal — the two of them are not risking the same amount, and both know it. The film comes from Umberto Saba's novel, and scholarship has since fixed on precisely that passage from page to screen: how much of the book's directness survives it, and what a 1979 production adjusted so the material would sit more comfortably. Salvatore Samperi keeps everything low and domestic. Ninety-eight minutes in rooms where nothing said aloud is quite the thing being discussed.

A herd of pigs on one bank, a river running fast, and a couple with no other offer of work in the city they fled to. The job is to get the animals across. They are there because an election in a village in northeastern India put a Dalit in the mayor's office and the killing that followed drove them off their own ground; Calcutta, when they reach it, gives them pavement to sleep on and no employer who needs them. She is pregnant. Goutam Ghose spends a hundred and forty-one minutes establishing how a person with nothing negotiates for less than nothing, and he films the labour rather than the meaning of the labour — bodies, animals, water, weight. Their poverty has a date and a cause, and the film puts both of them in the first reel.

The premise is deliberately thin: a man whose wife has left him, a job in another country, an evening in a bar. François Combe is a French actor now working for a New York television company; Kay Larsi is the woman he meets there, and the film gives her no more introduction than that. Marcel Carné sets the story in America and keeps everything else French — the tempo, the talk, the conviction that two people going through a night together is sufficient material for a hundred and ten minutes. Most of it happens in rooms after midnight, in the negotiation over how much of a past to hand across and when. What the film is testing is whether honesty can come before attachment, or whether it only ever arrives afterwards, in the form of an apology.

Northern Norway in summer does not go dark, so a father and son in a car have nowhere to put the silence. He has been absent for years and has decided, late, to do something about it; the something is a drive. Thomas Arslan builds the film out of the material most road pictures cut — the road itself, the pauses, the stretches in which neither passenger says a line worth quoting afterwards. Eighty-six minutes, two people in adjacent seats, one of whom did not ask for any of this. The son is under no obligation to reward the attempt, and the film will not hurry him toward forgiveness on the schedule his father would prefer. Repair is being attempted without a shared vocabulary, in a landscape that offers no cover and no way to look busy.

On 16 March 1978 the Red Brigades took Aldo Moro, and the Italian state discovered how much of its authority had rested on nobody testing it. Moro led the Christian Democrats, the party that had governed since the end of the war, which made his captivity a problem for every institution at once. Giuseppe Ferrara's account is deliberately unheated: a reconstruction of the fifty-five days that follows the meetings and the decisions rather than the gunfire, and that trusts the sequence of events to be dramatic enough without underlining. It was made in 1987, nine years on, for an audience that had lived through the whole thing. A hundred and twelve minutes, and the tension comes from watching men in rooms decide what they are prepared to do, and how long they can take deciding it.
